| Infrastructure providers | DigitalOcean, Vultr, Linode, AWS, Google Compute Engine |
| Control panel | Cloudways' own proprietary dashboard (no cPanel) |
| Risk-free trial | Short free trial, no credit card required |
| Free migration | Yes, included |
| Best for | Developers, agencies, and store owners who want managed cloud servers without sysadmin work |

## What Cloudways actually is

Cloudways doesn't own or run data centers. It's a management layer that sits on top of infrastructure from five separate cloud providers — you pick DigitalOcean, Vultr, Linode, AWS, or Google Compute Engine (GCE) at signup, and Cloudways provisions a server there, then handles the parts a typical hosting customer doesn't want to do themselves: server hardening, security patching, caching configuration, automated backups, one-click installs for WordPress, WooCommerce, Magento and Laravel, staging environments, and a team-management dashboard.

This is a meaningfully different model from a shared host like Hostinger or Namecheap. You're not buying a slice of a shared server on a flat monthly plan — you're renting a cloud instance from a named provider, with Cloudways charging its own management fee layered on top of what that provider would otherwise charge for the same box. That's also why there's no cPanel: Cloudways built its own dashboard because it needs to manage servers across five different backends through one consistent interface, and cPanel isn't designed for that.

## Pricing by infrastructure provider

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — check Cloudways' own pricing page for current figures before buying.

| Provider | Entry-level price | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| DigitalOcean | ~$11/month | ~2GB RAM, 1 vCPU, 50GB storage, 2TB transfer |
| Vultr | ~$14/month | Comparable entry specs, slightly pricier base rate |
| Linode | ~$14/month | Comparable entry specs, slightly pricier base rate |
| AWS | ~$20+/month | Higher compute cost passed through from AWS's own pricing |
| Google Compute Engine | ~$37+/month | Highest entry cost of the five, reflecting GCE's own rates |

DigitalOcean is consistently the cheapest way into Cloudways and is what most reviewers and Cloudways itself lead with in marketing. AWS and GCE cost more not because Cloudways charges more for its management layer on those providers, but because AWS and GCE themselves charge more for comparable compute than DigitalOcean, Vultr or Linode do.

## The real cost breakdown

The advertised ~$11/month DigitalOcean entry price is a starting point, not a ceiling — this is the single most important thing to understand about Cloudways before signing up. Because billing is usage-based:

- Bandwidth beyond your server's included transfer allowance is billed as an overage.
- Scaling RAM, storage or vCPU up (which you'll likely need to do as traffic grows) increases the monthly bill directly, unlike a fixed hosting plan where you simply hit a hard cap.
- Add-ons like a dedicated IP, additional staging apps, backup retention beyond the default window, and Cloudways' own CDN are billed separately.
- There's no long-term promotional pricing model here the way there is with shared hosts — you're not locking in a 24-48 month rate to get a lower headline number; the usage-based number you see is close to what you'll actually pay in a normal month, assuming you don't spike in traffic or storage.

Cloudways does not advertise a traditional money-back guarantee. Instead, it offers a short free trial (no credit card required) to test the platform, server performance, and your actual app's resource footprint before you commit any money. Use that window seriously — it's your only real chance to validate the cost assumption before billing starts.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose DigitalOcean's entry tier** if you're running one WordPress or WooCommerce site with modest traffic and want the cheapest reasonable entry point into managed cloud hosting.
- **Choose Vultr or Linode** if you have a specific reason to prefer their network/region footprint over DigitalOcean's, since pricing is close enough that it usually comes down to that rather than cost.
- **Choose AWS** if your team or client already has AWS infrastructure elsewhere and wants hosting to live in the same ecosystem, or needs an AWS-specific region/compliance posture.
- **Choose Google Compute Engine** if you specifically need GCE, otherwise its higher entry cost is hard to justify over DigitalOcean for an equivalent workload.
- **Scale up server size, not just add servers,** as a single site's traffic grows — Cloudways makes vertical scaling (bumping RAM/vCPU on an existing server) straightforward from its dashboard.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Choice of five real infrastructure providers, not locked to one | No cPanel — has a learning curve if you're used to it |
| Managed layer handles patching, caching, backups, staging | Usage-based billing means the bill isn't fixed month to month |
| Free migration included | No traditional money-back guarantee, only a short free trial |
| Genuinely strong Trustpilot reputation | AWS/GCE entry pricing is noticeably higher than DigitalOcean/Vultr/Linode |
| One dashboard across all five providers | Not aimed at total beginners — assumes some comfort with server concepts |

## Support

Cloudways offers live chat and ticket-based support as its primary channels, with the depth of assistance generally described as more technically capable than typical budget shared-hosting support, reflecting its developer/agency-leaning customer base. As with any host, actual response times can vary by plan tier and time of day — check current SLAs on Cloudways' own site if support responsiveness is a deciding factor for you.

## Migration

Cloudways includes free website migration from your existing host, with its team handling the move. This is a genuine advantage over hosts that charge for migration or leave you to do it yourself, and it removes one of the biggest friction points in switching hosts — especially relevant here since you're also switching away from cPanel to Cloudways' own dashboard, so having their team handle the technical transfer matters more than usual.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Developers and agencies managing multiple client sites who want one dashboard across different cloud providers.
- Store owners and businesses that have outgrown shared hosting's shared-resource limits but don't want to manage raw cloud servers themselves.
- Anyone who wants the option to choose infrastructure provider (or switch between them) without changing management tools.

## Where to think twice

- Complete beginners who want the simplicity and predictability of a flat monthly hosting bill — usage-based billing adds a variable you have to actually monitor.
- Sites with a habit of unpredictable traffic spikes, where bandwidth overages could turn a $11 base price into something meaningfully higher without warning.
- Anyone specifically wanting cPanel, since Cloudways' dashboard is a different (if arguably more modern) interface with its own learning curve.

## Bottom line

Cloudways is a legitimate, well-regarded option for managed cloud hosting once you understand what you're actually buying: not a flat-rate hosting plan, but a management layer on top of real cloud infrastructure, billed on usage. The entry price is genuinely competitive against comparable managed cloud options, the choice of five providers is a real advantage over single-provider managed hosts, and the Trustpilot track record backs up the reputation. The tradeoff is billing predictability — if you want to know your exact hosting cost every month without checking a usage dashboard, a flat-tier shared host will serve that need better than Cloudways will.

## FAQs

**Does Cloudways offer a money-back guarantee?**
No traditional money-back guarantee is advertised. Cloudways instead offers a short free trial (no credit card required) so you can test the platform and estimate real usage costs before paying anything.

**Is Cloudways more expensive than shared hosting?**
Its entry price (~$11/month on DigitalOcean) is competitive with mid-tier shared hosting, but because billing is usage-based rather than flat, your actual monthly cost can end up higher than a comparable shared-hosting plan once you factor in bandwidth, storage and add-ons.

**Which infrastructure provider is cheapest on Cloudways?**
DigitalOcean has the lowest entry-level pricing among the five providers Cloudways supports (DigitalOcean, Vultr, Linode, AWS, Google Compute Engine), with Vultr and Linode close behind and AWS/GCE noticeably higher.

**Does Cloudways use cPanel?**
No. Cloudways built its own proprietary dashboard to manage servers consistently across all five supported infrastructure providers, rather than using cPanel or Plesk.

**Does Cloudways migrate my existing site for free?**
Yes, Cloudways includes free migration from your current host as part of onboarding.

**Is Cloudways good for beginners?**
It's usable by beginners but leans toward developers and agencies — the usage-based billing model and the absence of a familiar cPanel interface mean there's more to learn upfront than with a flat-rate shared host.

**Can I switch infrastructure providers later on Cloudways?**
Cloudways' whole model is built around giving you a choice of provider at signup and letting you manage servers across providers from one dashboard, which is one of its main differentiators from single-provider managed hosts.

**What happens if my site's traffic spikes on Cloudways?**
Because billing is usage-based, a traffic spike that pushes you past your server's included bandwidth allowance will show up as a billed overage rather than the site simply being throttled the way some shared-hosting caps work — budget for this if your traffic is unpredictable.

Ready to compare pricing directly? Check the [Cloudways coupon page](/coupons/cloudways) for current offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: Contabo Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Contabo packs high RAM/CPU specs into cheap VPS plans but skips cPanel. Here's the real pricing, support quality and who it actually fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Contabo worth it?

Contabo is worth it if you want raw compute — VPS or dedicated server resources — at some of the lowest prices per GB of RAM in the industry, and you're comfortable managing Linux yourself. It's not worth it if you want managed shared hosting with cPanel included, since Contabo ships plans without any control panel by default.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | €5.50/mo (Cloud VPS 4: 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM, 100GB SSD) |
| Top entry-level tier | €49/mo (Cloud VPS 18: 18 vCPU, 96GB RAM, 600GB SSD) |
| Billing model | Effective monthly rate on a 24-month term; 1-month minimum contract available at a higher rate |
| Control panel | None bundled — raw server, self-managed |
| Money-back window | 14 days (private accounts; domains excluded) |
| Data centers | ~11 locations: US, UK, Europe, Singapore, Japan, India, Australia |
| Best for | Developers, self-hosters, and budget-conscious teams who don't need a GUI |

## What Contabo actually is

Contabo is a German infrastructure provider selling cloud VPS instances and dedicated servers — not managed shared hosting. There's no shared cPanel account, no pre-installed WordPress environment, and no support agent installing your CMS for you. You get root access to a Linux (or Windows) box and you're expected to configure it: install a web server, a database, TLS certificates, and — if you want one — a control panel of your own choosing.

This distinction matters because Contabo's headline appeal is specs-per-dollar: its entry Cloud VPS 4 plan ships with 8GB of RAM and 4 vCPUs for €5.50/month, which is well above what similarly priced shared-hosting or even many other VPS plans offer. That headroom exists precisely because Contabo isn't also selling you a managed panel, a support team that fixes your PHP config, or guaranteed dedicated (non-shared) CPU cycles at every tier — it's closer to a budget cloud-compute vendor than a traditional web host.

## Pricing

| Plan | vCPU | RAM | Storage | Effective price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cloud VPS 4 | 4 | 8 GB | 100 GB SSD | €5.50/mo |
| Cloud VPS 6 | 6 | 12 GB | 200 GB SSD | €7.50/mo |
| Cloud VPS 8 | 8 | 24 GB | 300 GB SSD | €14.00/mo |
| Cloud VPS 12 | 12 | 48 GB | 400 GB SSD | €25.00/mo |
| Cloud VPS 16 | 16 | 64 GB | 500 GB SSD | €37.00/mo |
| Cloud VPS 18 | 18 | 96 GB | 600 GB SSD | €49.00/mo |

All tiers include unlimited traffic, DDoS protection, a firewall, and dedicated IPv4/IPv6 addresses. Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check Contabo's own VPS pricing page for the current live rate before ordering.

## The real cost breakdown

The prices above are the *effective monthly rate on a 24-month subscription* — the number Contabo advertises up front. The minimum commitment is actually just one month, but choosing a shorter term (1, 3, 6 or 12 months) costs noticeably more per month than committing to two years; Contabo doesn't publish a single flat "renewal shock" the way some shared hosts do, but the underlying mechanic is the same idea — the longer term you prepay, the lower the effective monthly number you see advertised. There's no bundled free domain, and no free daily backups at the entry tiers; snapshot/backup add-ons, extra IPv4 addresses, and managed OS licensing (e.g., Windows Server) are priced separately at checkout. Budget for those add-ons before assuming the sticker price is your final cost.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Cloud VPS 4 (€5.50/mo)** — a single self-hosted app, a small Node/Python API, a lightweight self-managed WordPress site, or a dev/staging box. 8GB of RAM is generous for this price tier.
- **Cloud VPS 6-8 (€7.50-€14/mo)** — a handful of low-to-medium traffic sites, a small team's internal tools, or a self-hosted database plus app server on one box.
- **Cloud VPS 12-16 (€25-€37/mo)** — resource-heavy workloads: multiple containerized services, a build/CI runner, a game server, or a small production cluster node.
- **Cloud VPS 18 (€49/mo)** — the top entry-level tier, suited to consolidating several production services or running memory-hungry workloads (large databases, ML inference, heavy caching layers) on one instance instead of paying cloud-provider per-GB rates.

If you specifically need cPanel, automatic backups, or a beginner GUI out of the box, a managed shared host (or a VPS provider that bundles a panel) will get you there faster, at the cost of paying more per GB of RAM.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Very high RAM/CPU/storage per euro versus most VPS competitors | No control panel bundled — self-management required |
| Strong overall Trustpilot rating (4.6/5 across 11,000+ reviews) | Meaningful share of 1-star reviews cite slow support response |
| Wide global data center footprint (~11 locations) | No free daily backups or domain included at entry tiers |
| Unlimited traffic and DDoS protection included on every plan | Effective price shown assumes a 24-month commitment |
| Short (14-day) refund window still available on private accounts | Shorter-term billing costs more per month than the advertised rate |

## Support

Contabo support skews genuinely mixed rather than uniformly good or bad. The aggregate Trustpilot picture is strongly positive — about 77% of reviewers give 5 stars, and many specifically credit responsive support — but roughly 11% leave 1-star reviews, and a recurring theme in that minority is slow or frustrating ticket response times, particularly for technical troubleshooting rather than billing questions. There's no live phone support advertised; support runs through a ticket system and a help-center knowledge base. If round-the-clock hands-on support is a hard requirement, treat this as a real trade-off rather than a rare exception — verify current response-time expectations before committing a production workload.

## Migration

Because Contabo sells raw compute rather than managed hosting, there's no white-glove "we'll move your site for you" migration service built into most plans — moving an existing site means provisioning the new VPS yourself, installing your stack, and transferring files/databases (via rsync, a backup/restore tool, or your CMS's own migration plugin) before repointing DNS. This is standard for any unmanaged VPS, but it's a meaningfully bigger lift than migrating between two shared-hosting cPanel accounts, so factor in the time (or the cost of hiring someone) if you're not comfortable with server administration yourself.

## Where it's a strong fit

Contabo makes sense for developers running self-hosted apps, small SaaS backends, game servers, CI/build runners, or personal infrastructure who want to maximize RAM and CPU per dollar and are comfortable configuring Linux themselves. It's also a reasonable fit for agencies or freelancers who already run their own hosting stack (Docker, a reverse proxy, their own panel like CyberPanel) and just need cheap, capable compute behind it.

## Where to think twice

Skip Contabo if you want cPanel out of the box, automatic daily backups included in the base price, phone support, or a beginner-friendly one-click WordPress setup — those needs are better served by a managed shared host. It's also worth pausing if your workload can't tolerate any support-response variability, given the mixed (though still net-positive) support feedback in Trustpilot reviews.

## Bottom line

Contabo delivers real, verifiable value on raw specs — more RAM and CPU per euro than most VPS competitors — in exchange for handling server administration yourself and accepting some inconsistency in support quality. For developers and self-managed users, that trade is usually worth it. For anyone who wants a control panel and hand-holding included, it isn't the right category of host to begin with.

Check current rates on the [Contabo coupon page](/coupons/contabo), or compare it against managed options on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

## FAQs

**Does Contabo include cPanel?**
No. Contabo VPS and dedicated server plans ship without any control panel. You install and manage your own (cPanel, Plesk, CyberPanel, or none at all) if you want one.

**What's the cheapest Contabo VPS plan?**
Cloud VPS 4, at an effective €5.50/month, includes 4 vCPUs, 8GB RAM and 100GB SSD storage — the entry point into Contabo's Cloud VPS lineup.

**Is the advertised Contabo price what I pay every month?**
The advertised rate is the effective monthly price on a 24-month term. Shorter billing terms (1, 3, 6 or 12 months) cost more per month than the headline number, so check the term-by-term pricing at checkout.

**Does Contabo offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — a 14-day revocation period for private accounts (domain purchases excluded), plus a separate window to request a refund within 72 hours of an unwanted automatic renewal.

**Is Contabo good for beginners?**
Generally no. Without a bundled control panel, Contabo expects some server-administration comfort. Beginners who want a simple dashboard experience are typically better served by managed shared hosting.

**Is Contabo reliable?**
Trustpilot data shows a strong 4.6/5 rating across more than 11,000 reviews, with most praising reliability and value for money — but a real minority report support and technical friction, so expectations should account for that variance.

**Where are Contabo's data centers located?**
Contabo operates roughly 11 data center locations worldwide, spanning the US, UK, continental Europe, Singapore, Japan, India and Australia.

**Can I migrate my existing site to Contabo myself?**
Yes, but there's no built-in managed migration service — you provision the VPS, install your stack, and transfer your site's files and database yourself (or hire someone to do it), then update DNS.

title: DigitalOcean Review 2026: Droplet Pricing and Verdict
excerpt: DigitalOcean's Droplet pricing, billing model, and who it actually fits — a developer-focused cloud host, not a beginner shared-hosting panel.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is DigitalOcean a good choice for hosting your site?

DigitalOcean is a cloud infrastructure provider, not a shared web host — it sells "Droplets," raw virtual servers billed by the hour or month based on RAM, CPU and storage. There's no bundled control panel. It's a strong pick for developers who can manage a Linux server themselves, and a poor fit for anyone wanting a beginner-friendly dashboard.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $4/month (512 MiB RAM, 1 vCPU, 10 GB SSD) |
| Billing model | Per-second, hourly or monthly, no long-term contract required |
| Control panel | None bundled — one-click app images available |
| Uptime guarantee | Not marketed as a shared-hosting-style SLA percentage |
| Money-back guarantee | No blanket refund policy; new accounts often get an intro credit instead |
| Best for | Developers, agencies, and self-managed apps/sites |

## What DigitalOcean actually is

DigitalOcean is cloud infrastructure, not managed website hosting. When you spin up a "Droplet," you get a virtual private server with root access and nothing else pre-installed beyond the OS image you pick. There's no cPanel, no hPanel, no built-in file manager or one-click WordPress installer baked into every plan by default — though DigitalOcean does offer a marketplace of one-click app images (WordPress, Docker, LAMP/LEMP stacks, and more) that install common software for you at Droplet creation.

That distinction matters because it changes who this is for. A shared host like Hostinger or Namecheap hands you a dashboard and handles the server underneath it. DigitalOcean hands you the server itself. You're responsible for installing a web server (Nginx or Apache), a database, an SSL certificate, firewall rules, and applying your own security updates — or layering a management tool (like a control panel you install yourself, or a platform like cPanel licensed separately) on top.

## Droplet pricing (accurate as of September 2026)

| Plan | RAM | vCPU | SSD storage | Transfer | Monthly | Hourly |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | 512 MiB | 1 | 10 GB | 500 GiB | $4.00 | $0.00595 |
| Basic | 1 GiB | 1 | 25 GB | 1,000 GiB | $6.00 | $0.00893 |
| Basic | 2 GiB | 1 | 50 GB | 2,000 GiB | $12.00 | $0.01786 |
| Basic | 2 GiB | 2 | 60 GB | 3,000 GiB | $18.00 | $0.02679 |

Pricing is pulled from DigitalOcean's own pricing page and was accurate as of this post's publish date — cloud pricing changes periodically, so confirm current rates before buying.

## The real cost breakdown

DigitalOcean bills per-second, with a 60-second minimum charge (or $0.01, whichever is higher), up to a monthly cap equal to the advertised monthly price. In practice that means:

- Run a $6/month Droplet for the full month and you pay $6.
- Run the same Droplet for 10 days and destroy it, and you pay roughly a third of that — not the full monthly rate.
- There's no multi-year contract or renewal-price trap the way shared hosts structure their pricing. What you see is what you pay, based on actual usage.

The cost risk to watch is bandwidth. Each Droplet includes a set transfer allowance (500 GiB–3,000 GiB on the entry tiers above); overage is billed per GiB beyond that. A low-traffic personal site or small app will rarely come close to the limit, but a media-heavy or high-traffic project can rack up transfer charges that a flat-rate shared-hosting plan wouldn't. New signups commonly get an introductory credit toward their first weeks of usage — the amount shown at signup can vary, so treat any number you see elsewhere as unconfirmed until you check it yourself during account creation.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose the $4/month Droplet** if you're running a small personal project, a lightweight API, or testing something that doesn't need to stay up 24/7 — the per-second billing means short-lived experiments cost pennies.
- **Choose the $6/month Droplet** for a single low-to-moderate-traffic website or blog where you want a bit more breathing room than the absolute minimum tier.
- **Choose the $12/month Droplet** if you're running a small production app, a WordPress site with meaningful traffic, or anything where 1 vCPU is starting to feel tight.
- **Choose the $18/month Droplet (2 vCPUs)** if your workload is CPU-bound — multiple services, a build pipeline, or an app under real concurrent load — rather than just needing more RAM.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Transparent per-second/hourly billing, no renewal-price trap | No bundled control panel — you manage the server |
| Full root access and flexibility to run anything | Requires Linux/server administration knowledge |
| One-click app images speed up common setups | Bandwidth overage is billed per GiB beyond the plan allowance |
| Scales up (more RAM/CPU) without migrating hosts | No shared-hosting-style money-back guarantee |
| Strong developer documentation and community tutorials | Not designed for non-technical beginners |

## Support

DigitalOcean offers ticket-based support plus an extensive public knowledge base and community Q&A ("DigitalOcean Community") with a large volume of user-contributed tutorials covering common server-setup tasks. Higher-tier paid support plans exist for teams that want faster response times or a dedicated technical account manager, but the baseline experience assumes you can troubleshoot a lot yourself using the documentation — there's no 24/7 live chat aimed at walking a beginner through fixing a broken WordPress install the way a shared host's support desk might.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to a Droplet is a manual, self-managed process: you provision the server, install your stack (or use a one-click image), then migrate files and databases over yourself — via command-line tools, backup/restore utilities, or a migration plugin if you're moving WordPress specifically. DigitalOcean doesn't offer a white-glove "we'll move your site for you" service the way some managed hosts do. If you're not comfortable with SSH, database dumps, and DNS cutover, budget time to learn this or hire someone who already knows it.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Developers and agencies who want full control over the server stack.
- Apps, APIs, or sites that need to scale compute resources independently of storage or bandwidth.
- Teams already comfortable with Linux administration who want predictable, usage-based pricing instead of a shared-hosting renewal cycle.
- Projects with variable/spiky traffic where per-second billing avoids paying for idle capacity.

## Where to think twice

- You want a beginner control panel with one-click everything and don't plan to touch a terminal.
- You need someone else to handle server security patches and uptime monitoring for you.
- You want a flat monthly bill with no risk of a bandwidth-overage surprise.
- You're launching a single small site and don't need the flexibility a raw server provides — a shared host will likely be cheaper and far less hands-on.

## Bottom line

DigitalOcean is a well-regarded, transparently priced cloud infrastructure provider — not a replacement for shared web hosting. If you can manage a Linux server (or are willing to learn), the per-second billing, straightforward pricing tiers, and lack of a renewal-price trap make it a genuinely good deal. If you want a dashboard that handles the server for you, look at a managed shared host instead; running a Droplet without that background will mean spending time on setup and maintenance that a shared-hosting control panel would otherwise handle automatically.

Compare it against a managed option on our [DigitalOcean coupon page](/coupons/digitalocean), or browse more options on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

## FAQs

**Does DigitalOcean include a free trial?**
New accounts commonly receive an introductory usage credit for their first weeks on the platform. The exact amount shown at signup can change over time, so check the current offer during account creation rather than relying on a number you saw elsewhere.

**Do I need to know Linux to use DigitalOcean?**
Not strictly, thanks to one-click app images that pre-install common software, but ongoing server management — security updates, firewall configuration, troubleshooting — assumes basic command-line comfort. It's not designed for a fully hands-off beginner experience.

**Is DigitalOcean cheaper than shared hosting?**
The entry-level Droplet ($4/month) undercuts many shared-hosting renewal prices, but that comparison isn't apples-to-apples — a shared host bundles a control panel and managed server administration into its price, while a Droplet is just compute you configure yourself.

**Does DigitalOcean offer a money-back guarantee?**
DigitalOcean doesn't advertise a blanket refund policy the way shared hosts typically do. Because billing is per-second/hourly, you're only charged for the time a Droplet actually runs rather than committing to a prepaid term upfront.

**Can I install WordPress on DigitalOcean?**
Yes, via a one-click WordPress app image that provisions a Droplet with WordPress, a web server and a database already installed — though you'll still be responsible for ongoing maintenance, backups and updates yourself.

**What happens if I go over my bandwidth allowance?**
Each Droplet includes a transfer allowance (500 GiB on the smallest tier, scaling up on larger plans); usage beyond that is billed per GiB. High-traffic or media-heavy sites should monitor usage to avoid surprise overage charges.

**Does DigitalOcean have data centers in multiple regions?**
Yes — DigitalOcean operates Droplets across multiple global regions, letting you pick one close to your users; available regions are listed during Droplet creation.

**Is DigitalOcean good for a small personal blog?**
It can work, but a blog with no need for custom server configuration usually gets more built-in convenience (backups, a dashboard, installers) from a managed shared host for similar cost. DigitalOcean makes more sense once you want server-level control.

title: Flywheel Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: An evidence-based look at Flywheel's managed WordPress hosting: real pricing, agency tools, migration, support and whether it's worth it in 2026.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Flywheel a good choice for WordPress hosting?

Flywheel is a managed, WordPress-only host owned by WP Engine and built for designers, freelancers and agencies rather than budget shoppers. It's a solid pick if you manage client sites and want billing-transfer and collaborator tools — a poor pick if you want cPanel, multi-platform hosting, or the cheapest possible plan.

| Quick fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Starting price | $30/month billed monthly, $25/month billed annually ($300/year) |
| Renewal price | Same rate structure continues; no separate teaser/renewal split reported |
| Control panel | Proprietary Flywheel dashboard (no cPanel) |
| Uptime guarantee | Not published on the pricing page |
| Money-back guarantee | 60 days (Starter and qualifying Freelance plans only) |
| Best for | WordPress agencies and freelancers managing multiple client sites |

## What Flywheel actually is

Flywheel is a managed WordPress hosting company that WP Engine acquired in 2019 and continues to run as a distinct brand aimed squarely at the design and agency market. It doesn't host anything other than WordPress, and it doesn't offer cPanel — everything runs through Flywheel's own dashboard, built around workflows like spinning up a new site, staging changes, and handing a finished project off to a client.

That agency focus shows up in features that generic shared hosts don't bother with: an "Organizations" structure for managing sites across a team, a "Collaborators" tool that gives a client or contractor secure access to a single site without exposing the rest of your account, "Billing Transfer" for moving a completed site's invoice over to the client once launch is done, and "Blueprints" for saving a site's configuration as a reusable starting point for future builds. None of this matters if you're hosting one personal blog — it matters a lot if you build WordPress sites for other people.

## Flywheel pricing

Pricing below reflects Flywheel's published plans as of this post's date (September 2026) and can change — check Flywheel's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Monthly billing | Annual billing | Sites | Storage | Monthly visits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | ~$30/mo | $25/mo ($300/yr) | 1 | 10GB | 25,000 |
| Freelance | ~$115/mo | $96/mo ($1,150/yr) | Up to 10 | 20GB | 100,000 |
| Agency | ~$290/mo | $242/mo ($2,900/yr) | Up to 30 | 50GB | 400,000 |
| Custom | Contact sales | Contact sales | 30+ | Custom | Millions+ |

Additional sites can be added to the Freelance or Agency plan for $20/month ($200/year each) rather than upgrading the whole plan a tier.

## The real cost of a Flywheel plan

The headline number that shows up in ads and comparison tables is usually the annual-billing rate — $25/month for Starter, for example — but that requires paying $300 upfront for the year, not $25 charged monthly. Pay month to month instead and Starter runs closer to $30/month, Freelance around $115/month, and Agency around $290/month. Unlike some budget hosts that use a low first-term "intro" price that jumps sharply at renewal, Flywheel's structure is simpler: the annual price is the discounted rate for prepaying a year, and it's the same rate you'd pay again the following year, not a one-time teaser. Migrations are included at no extra cost on every plan, which offsets some of the higher entry price if you're moving existing sites in rather than building fresh.

Where the real cost creeps in is site count and traffic. Outgrow the Starter plan's single site or 25,000 monthly visits and you're either adding a $20/month site add-on or upgrading a full tier — a jump from $25/month to $96/month annually is a real budget decision, not a rounding error.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose **Starter** if you're launching or maintaining exactly one WordPress site — a portfolio, a small business site, or a single client project — and don't expect to exceed 25,000 visits a month.

Choose **Freelance** if you're a freelancer or small studio juggling a handful of client sites (up to 10) and want the Collaborators and Billing Transfer tools to hand finished sites off cleanly without sharing your whole account.

Choose **Agency** if you're running a larger book of client work — up to 30 sites — and need the higher traffic ceiling (400,000 monthly visits) and storage (50GB) that come with it, and can absorb the loss of the 60-day money-back guarantee that this tier doesn't carry.

Choose **Custom** only once you've outgrown Agency's 30-site cap or need bespoke server resources; this tier is quote-based rather than self-serve.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Free migrations on every plan | WordPress-only — no other CMS or general-purpose hosting |
| Genuine agency tools (Collaborators, Billing Transfer, Blueprints, Organizations) | No cPanel — a learning curve if your workflow depends on it |
| Straightforward annual-vs-monthly pricing (no aggressive renewal-price jump) | Entry price is high next to budget shared hosts like Hostinger or Namecheap |
| 60-day money-back guarantee on entry-level plans | Guarantee excludes Agency and Custom plans, and all upgrades/renewals |
| Owned by WP Engine, a large established managed-WordPress operator | Trustpilot reviews for the brand skew heavily negative |

## Support

Flywheel's support is delivered through its own dashboard and ticket/chat system rather than a generic hosting help desk, and it's scoped to WordPress specifically — the team isn't fielding questions about other CMSes or general server administration. Response quality and speed are the most commonly cited complaint in third-party reviews of the brand, so if support responsiveness is a dealbreaker for you, weigh that against the platform's other strengths before committing to an annual plan.

## Migrating to Flywheel

Every plan tier includes free migration of existing WordPress sites, handled by Flywheel's own migration team rather than a self-service plugin you run yourself. That's a meaningful convenience if you're moving several client sites over at once, since it removes one of the more error-prone parts of a hosting switch. There's no published cap on how many sites this covers per plan beyond the plan's own site-count limit.

## Where it's a strong fit

Flywheel makes the most sense for freelancers and agencies who exclusively build on WordPress, manage multiple client properties, and would actually use the Collaborators/Billing Transfer/Blueprints workflow — these are real, non-generic features that solve a specific agency problem (handing off a site to a client without handing off your whole hosting account).

## Where to think twice

Skip Flywheel if you need cPanel, host anything besides WordPress, or are price-sensitive and comparing against budget shared hosts — the entry-level Starter plan costs several times what a basic Hostinger or Namecheap shared plan runs, for a single site. The heavily negative Trustpilot review pattern is also worth weighing directly rather than dismissing, since it's a large enough sample to reflect a real support/experience pattern for at least a subset of customers.

## Bottom line

Flywheel is a purpose-built managed WordPress host for agencies, not a general hosting recommendation. The pricing structure is honest in that the annual rate doesn't balloon at renewal the way some budget hosts' promotional pricing does, and the agency-specific tooling is genuinely useful if you manage client sites for a living. But it's WordPress-only, meaningfully pricier than budget shared hosting at the entry tier, and the public review record on Trustpilot is poor enough that it deserves real weight in the decision — read a sample of the negative reviews yourself before committing to an annual plan.

## FAQs

**Is Flywheel good for beginners?**
Flywheel is built for people already building on WordPress professionally, not first-time website owners — there's no cPanel, no support for other platforms, and pricing starts well above typical beginner shared-hosting plans.

**Does Flywheel offer cPanel?**
No. Flywheel uses its own proprietary hosting dashboard for all site and account management instead of cPanel.

**What does Flywheel's money-back guarantee actually cover?**
A 60-day window applies only to new Starter plans and Freelance plans that don't include custom onboarding. Agency plans, Custom plans, and any plan upgrade or renewal are explicitly excluded.

**Does Flywheel charge more at renewal than the advertised price?**
Not in the way many budget hosts do with a steep introductory-to-renewal jump. The annual-billing rate (e.g., $25/month for Starter) is a discount for prepaying a year and continues at the same rate on renewal; paying monthly instead runs closer to $30/month from the start.

**Is Flywheel only for WordPress?**
Yes. Flywheel is a WordPress-only managed host and doesn't support other content management systems or general-purpose hosting.

**Does Flywheel migrate existing sites for free?**
Yes, every plan includes free migration of your site(s) handled by Flywheel's own team.

**What are Flywheel's Collaborators and Billing Transfer tools?**
Collaborators grants a client or teammate secure access to a single site without exposing your full Flywheel account. Billing Transfer lets you hand a finished site's billing over to the client once a project is complete — both are aimed at agencies managing client work rather than personal sites.

**How does Flywheel compare on price to budget hosts?**
It's substantially more expensive at the entry level than budget shared hosts. Compare current rates on the [Flywheel coupon page](/coupons/flywheel) and browse other options on [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) before deciding if the agency-specific tooling is worth the premium for your use case.

title: Hetzner Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Hetzner offers cheap, developer-focused cloud servers with no bundled control panel. Here's real pricing, data center coverage, and who it fits.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Hetzner good for hosting?

Hetzner is a strong choice if you're comfortable managing your own server — its cloud plans pack more CPU, RAM and storage per euro than almost any mainstream competitor. It's a poor choice if you want cPanel, one-click WordPress installs, or hand-holding support, since Hetzner sells raw compute, not managed shared hosting.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | €3.99/month (CX23: 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 40GB NVMe) |
| Billing model | Hourly, no long-term contract required |
| Control panel | None bundled — self-managed, install your own |
| Cancellation | Instant, from the Cloud Console |
| Data centers | Germany, Finland, US (Ashburn, Hillsboro), Singapore |
| Best for | Developers, self-hosters, budget-conscious VPS buyers |

## What Hetzner actually is

Hetzner is a German infrastructure company that owns and operates its own data centers rather than reselling capacity from a larger cloud vendor — a big part of why its per-spec pricing runs so far below AWS, DigitalOcean or even other budget hosts. It sells two main product lines: Cloud (on-demand virtual servers, billed hourly) and dedicated/root servers (physical machines, billed monthly).

This is not shared hosting in the traditional sense. There's no bundled cPanel or hPanel, no pre-installed WordPress, and no "click a button to launch a site" workflow. You choose an OS image (Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky Linux, and others), get root/SSH access, and configure the server yourself — or install a control panel of your own choosing (Plesk is available as a paid add-on through Hetzner's marketplace apps, but nothing is bundled by default). If that sounds like more setup than you want, Hetzner isn't the right fit; if you're comfortable with a terminal, it's one of the better price-to-spec ratios available.

## Pricing

Pricing below is quoted for Hetzner's German/Finnish data centers; US locations (Ashburn, Hillsboro) run roughly 20% higher. All prices are in EUR since that's how Hetzner bills.

| Plan | vCPU | RAM | Storage | Monthly price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CX23 | 2 | 4GB | 40GB NVMe | €3.99 |
| CX33 | 4 | 8GB | 80GB NVMe | €6.49 |
| CX43 | 8 | 16GB | 160GB NVMe | €11.99 |
| CX53 | 16 | 32GB | 320GB NVMe | €22.49 |
| CAX11 (ARM) | 2 | 4GB | 40GB NVMe | €4.49 |

All plans include 20TB of monthly traffic. Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and is subject to change — check Hetzner's live pricing page before buying, since Hetzner has adjusted prices more than once in 2026.

## The real cost breakdown

Hetzner's advertised prices are close to what you'll actually pay, which is a meaningful difference from shared-hosting providers that lean on multi-year introductory pricing. A few things to add to the sticker price, though:

- **IPv4 surcharge**: Hetzner unbundled primary IPv4 addresses in 2024 — each one now costs an extra €0.50/month, whether or not it's attached to a running server. IPv6 is free.
- **No long-term discount trap, but also no long-term discount**: billing is hourly (capped at the monthly rate), so there's no "renews at 3x the intro price" surprise — but there's also no reward for prepaying years in advance the way some shared hosts offer.
- **Backups and snapshots** cost extra if you enable them (typically a percentage of the server's base price), and aren't included by default.
- **Support** is community/ticket-based at this price point — there's no phone line, and priority support tiers cost more.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose CX23** if you're running a single small app, a personal site, or a low-traffic API — 4GB of RAM is enough for a lean Node.js, Python or PHP stack behind Nginx.
- **Choose CX33** if you're self-hosting something with a database alongside the app (WordPress + MySQL, a small SaaS backend) and want headroom before you start swapping.
- **Choose CX43 or CX53** if you're consolidating several sites/services on one box, running a CI runner, or hosting something with real concurrent traffic.
- **Choose the CAX (ARM) line** if your stack is ARM-compatible (most modern Docker images and interpreted languages are) and you want slightly better performance-per-euro on compute-bound workloads.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Very low price per vCPU/RAM/storage vs. mainstream clouds | No bundled control panel — self-managed only |
| Hourly billing, cancel anytime, no lock-in | Support is ticket-based, no phone line at this tier |
| Runs its own data centers (no reseller markup) | Limited global footprint outside EU/US-East/US-West/Singapore |
| Simple, transparent per-resource pricing | IPv4 costs extra; backups/snapshots are add-ons |
| Good fit for Docker, self-hosted apps, dev/test environments | Trustpilot rating sits at 3.0/5 — mixed sentiment, partly reflecting Hetzner's stricter fraud/abuse account reviews |

## Support

Hetzner's support is primarily ticket-based, backed by an extensive self-service documentation library (docs.hetzner.com) covering server setup, networking, and the Cloud API. There's no live phone support for standard Cloud accounts, and community forums fill in a lot of the practical troubleshooting knowledge. This works fine for the technical audience Hetzner targets, but it's a real gap if you're used to 24/7 live chat from a shared host.

## Migration

Moving an existing site to Hetzner is a manual process — there's no one-click site importer or "we'll migrate your WordPress for you" service typical of shared hosting. In practice this means either standing up a fresh server and manually copying files/databases over (rsync, mysqldump, etc.), or using a snapshot/image if you're moving between two cloud providers with compatible tooling. Budget real time for this if you're coming from a managed host with an automated migration path — Hetzner doesn't replicate that convenience.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Developers who want raw compute at a low price and are comfortable configuring their own stack.
- Self-hosted apps, Docker/Kubernetes workloads, CI runners, and dev/test environments where uptime SLAs matter less than cost.
- EU-based projects, or projects with a primarily EU/German audience, where Hetzner's home-turf data centers minimize latency.
- Anyone who wants to avoid the shared-hosting pattern of low introductory pricing followed by a much higher renewal rate.

## Where to think twice

- Beginners who want a managed dashboard, one-click WordPress, or phone support — Hetzner offers none of these by default.
- Projects with a primarily US, Latin American, African, or broader Asia-Pacific audience outside Singapore's reach, where Hetzner's thin data center footprint could add latency versus a host with more regional points of presence.
- Anyone who needs guaranteed account continuity for high-risk verticals — Hetzner is known for strict fraud/compliance reviews that can suspend accounts pending verification, which shows up in some of its lower Trustpilot reviews.

## Bottom line

Hetzner delivers genuinely excellent price-to-spec ratios for cloud compute, backed by its own data centers rather than resold capacity — that's the real draw, and it's a legitimate reason developers keep choosing it over pricier mainstream clouds. But it's infrastructure, not a beginner hosting product: there's no control panel, support is ticket-based, and its data center footprint is thin outside Europe, the US coasts, and Singapore. If you can administer a Linux server yourself and your audience is well-served by those regions, it's hard to beat on price. If you want a dashboard and hand-holding, look at a managed shared host instead.

## FAQs

**Does Hetzner include a free domain?**
No. Hetzner sells compute and infrastructure, not domain registration bundled with hosting plans. You'll need to register a domain separately and point it at your server's IP.

**Is Hetzner good for WordPress?**
It can host WordPress well if you're comfortable setting up the LEMP/LAMP stack yourself or using a pre-built image, but it doesn't offer the one-click WordPress installs or managed WordPress features that shared hosts and dedicated WordPress hosts provide.

**Does Hetzner offer a money-back guarantee?**
Cloud servers bill hourly and can be cancelled instantly with no penalty, so there's no need for a traditional refund window in most cases. EU customers also have the statutory 14-day right of withdrawal on new contracts.

**Why is Hetzner's Trustpilot rating only 3.0 out of 5?**
Hetzner's rating reflects a mix of very satisfied technical users praising the price/performance and a smaller number of complaints tied to account verification holds and support response times — common friction points for a low-margin infrastructure provider rather than signs of unreliable hardware.

**Does Hetzner charge extra for an IP address?**
Yes. Since 2024, a primary IPv4 address costs €0.50/month extra on Cloud servers; IPv6 addresses remain free.

**Is Hetzner cheaper than DigitalOcean or AWS?**
Generally yes, for comparable specs — Hetzner's core appeal is that it owns its own data centers rather than reselling capacity, which lets it price meaningfully below hyperscale and boutique clouds at the same vCPU/RAM tier.

**Can I use Hetzner if I'm outside Europe?**
Yes — Hetzner has data centers in Ashburn, Virginia and Hillsboro, Oregon for US customers, and Singapore for Asia-Pacific, though its overall global footprint is smaller than major hyperscalers, so check latency from your specific audience first.

**Do I need Linux experience to use Hetzner?**
It helps significantly. Since there's no bundled control panel, you'll be managing the server over SSH — comfortable with basic Linux administration is close to a prerequisite for a good experience.

Check the [Hetzner coupon page](/coupons/hetzner) for current offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: Hostwinds Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Hostwinds review covering cPanel shared hosting and VPS pricing, the 72-hour refund window, plans, support, and who it fits best.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Hostwinds a good hosting choice in 2026?

Hostwinds works best if you want cheap cPanel shared hosting with a modest gap between intro and renewal pricing, or if you want to grow into managed/unmanaged VPS and dedicated servers under the same account. It's a weaker pick if you value a long money-back window — Hostwinds gives you just 72 hours, pro-rated, not the 30-day guarantee most competitors offer.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $3.24/mo (Basic shared, longest term) |
| Renewal price | $6.99/mo (Basic shared) |
| Control panel | cPanel (shared); custom/no panel option on unmanaged VPS |
| Uptime guarantee | Not independently verified — see note below |
| Money-back guarantee | 72 hours, pro-rated only |
| Best for | Budget cPanel sites that may later need VPS/dedicated resources |

## What Hostwinds actually is

Hostwinds is a Seattle, Washington-based hosting company that's been running since 2010. Unlike hosts that specialize narrowly, Hostwinds sells two genuinely different product lines under one roof: cPanel-based shared hosting for small sites, and a separate, fairly extensive lineup of managed and unmanaged Linux/Windows VPS plans plus dedicated servers. That combination matters if you expect to outgrow shared hosting — you can move up within the same provider instead of migrating elsewhere.

Shared hosting comes in three tiers, all built on the standard cPanel interface rather than a custom dashboard, so anything you've learned managing cPanel elsewhere transfers directly.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — always confirm current rates on Hostwinds' own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Domains | Intro price | Renewal price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | 1 domain | $3.24/mo | $6.99/mo |
| Advanced | Up to 6 domains | $4.54/mo | $8.99/mo |
| Ultimate | Unlimited domains | $5.84/mo | $10.99/mo |

All three tiers advertise unlimited SSD storage and bandwidth, free SSL, a free dedicated IP, unlimited email accounts, and Softaculous one-click installs. None of the tiers include a free domain — you buy that separately, which is a real cost difference versus hosts that bundle one in for the first year.

Hostwinds' VPS line starts noticeably cheaper on the unmanaged side — entry configurations (roughly 1 CPU, 1GB RAM, 30GB SSD, 1TB bandwidth) run from around $4.99/month unmanaged or $7.14/month managed, scaling up into higher-core, higher-RAM tiers priced well into the hundreds of dollars per month. Windows VPS costs more at every tier to cover Windows Server licensing.

## The real cost breakdown

The advertised $3.24/$4.54/$5.84 rates require locking into Hostwinds' longest available billing term — shorter terms cost more per month from day one. When that term ends, the same plans renew at $6.99/$8.99/$10.99/month. That roughly-doubling jump is smaller than what some budget hosts do (where renewal can be 3-4x the intro rate), but it's still a real increase to budget for, and you should multiply the renewal rate by your term length before assuming the checkout price is what you'll pay long-term.

Because there's no free domain bundled in, add typical registration/renewal domain costs (usually $10-20/year depending on TLD) on top of whichever hosting tier you pick. SSL is free either way since Hostwinds includes it on every shared plan.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Basic** if you're hosting exactly one site — a portfolio, a small business page, a single WordPress blog — and don't need room to add more domains later.
- **Choose Advanced** if you manage a handful of sites (up to six) for yourself or a couple of clients and want headroom without paying for unlimited domains you won't use.
- **Choose Ultimate** if you run an agency-style setup or plan to keep adding sites over time; unlimited domains means you won't need to upgrade tiers again for that reason.
- **Choose VPS instead of shared** if a single site needs dedicated resources, custom software, or root access that shared hosting's shared-server model can't give you — Hostwinds' unmanaged VPS tiers are priced close to shared hosting at the entry level.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Runs on standard cPanel, not a custom panel | Only a 72-hour, pro-rated refund window |
| Unlimited storage/bandwidth on all shared tiers | No free domain on any plan |
| Smaller renewal-price jump than some budget hosts | Trustpilot rating is polarized (heavy 5-star and 1-star split) |
| Also offers VPS/dedicated for growth beyond shared | Longest term required to get the lowest advertised rate |
| Free dedicated IP included on shared plans | Domains, SSL, and hourly services are non-refundable |

## Support

Hostwinds advertises 24/7 support via live chat, phone, and ticket. Independent reviews describe support staff as generally knowledgeable, particularly for account and billing questions, though response quality on technical VPS/server issues varies more than on shared-hosting basics. There's no dedicated phone line separation by product tier — the same channels cover shared, VPS, and dedicated customers.

## Migration

Hostwinds' shared hosting runs cPanel, so migrating an existing cPanel-based site typically means a cPanel-to-cPanel account transfer, which Hostwinds' support can assist with. Moving into or out of a VPS is more manual — since unmanaged VPS gives you root access rather than a pre-configured stack, migrating a live site there usually means handling the server setup and file transfer yourself unless you pay for managed support.

## Where it's a strong fit

Hostwinds fits budget-conscious users who want plain cPanel shared hosting without a huge intro-to-renewal price cliff, and especially anyone who anticipates eventually needing a VPS or dedicated server and would rather not switch providers to get one. The unlimited-domain Ultimate tier is also a reasonable fit for small agencies juggling several low-traffic client sites on one account.

## Where to think twice

Skip Hostwinds if a long, no-risk trial window matters to you — 72 hours pro-rated is a fraction of the 30-day guarantee that's now standard at most competing hosts, so you have very little time to properly test a site's real-world performance before you're financially committed. The mixed Trustpilot record (strong on some support interactions, weak on billing/refund complaints) is also worth weighing if customer-service consistency is a priority. If you specifically want a bundled free domain in your first year's hosting cost, look elsewhere — Hostwinds doesn't include one.

## Bottom line

Hostwinds is a reasonable budget cPanel host with the added flexibility of an in-house VPS and dedicated-server line to grow into, and its renewal pricing isn't as punishing as some competitors'. The tradeoffs are real, though: a 72-hour pro-rated refund window instead of a 30-day guarantee, no free domain, and a Trustpilot record that swings between very satisfied and very unsatisfied customers. It's worth considering for a low-cost single or multi-site cPanel setup, but check the refund terms and your renewal math before committing to a long promotional term.

## FAQs

**Does Hostwinds offer shared hosting or just VPS?**
Both. Hostwinds sells cPanel-based shared hosting (Basic, Advanced, Ultimate tiers) as well as a separate line of managed and unmanaged Linux/Windows VPS plans and dedicated servers.

**What is Hostwinds' money-back guarantee?**
Only 72 hours from the payment transaction, and the refund is pro-rated for the unused portion of the service — not a full refund, and not the 30-day window many other hosts offer.

**Does Hostwinds include a free domain?**
No. None of Hostwinds' shared hosting tiers bundle a free domain; it must be purchased separately.

**Is Hostwinds' lowest advertised price what I'll pay long-term?**
No. The lowest rates require the longest signup term and increase on renewal (e.g. Basic goes from $3.24/month to $6.99/month) — factor the renewal rate into your decision, not just the checkout price.

**Does Hostwinds use cPanel?**
Yes, for all shared hosting plans. VPS and dedicated servers can be provisioned with or without a control panel depending on what you choose.

**What do Hostwinds reviews say about support?**
Reviews are mixed — many praise responsive, knowledgeable chat and phone support, while a notable share of negative reviews focus on billing and refund-related frustrations rather than technical support quality.

**Can I upgrade from shared hosting to a VPS later?**
Yes. Because Hostwinds runs both product lines itself, you can move from a shared plan to a VPS or dedicated server without switching providers, though migrating an existing site still takes manual setup work on unmanaged VPS tiers.

**Is Hostwinds good for beginners?**
The shared hosting side is beginner-friendly thanks to standard cPanel and one-click Softaculous installs. The VPS side, especially unmanaged plans, assumes more server-administration comfort and is less suited to first-time hosting users.

Ready to compare pricing directly? Check the [Hostwinds coupon page](/coupons/hostwinds) for current offers, or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) before you decide.

title: Kamatera Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Kamatera offers fully customizable cloud VPS pricing from $4/month and a 30-day trial — but no bundled control panel. Here's the full breakdown.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Kamatera Review 2026: Is This Cloud VPS Provider Worth It?

Kamatera is a cloud VPS host that prices CPU, RAM, storage and bandwidth as separate dials instead of fixed bundles, starting at $4/month, with hourly billing and a 30-day free trial worth up to $100. It suits developers and sysadmins comfortable managing a bare server — it does not include cPanel or any control panel by default.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $4/month (1 vCPU, 1GB RAM, 20GB NVMe SSD, 5TB traffic) |
| Billing model | Monthly (prepaid, prorated) or hourly (by the minute) |
| Control panel | None bundled — bare server image, install your own |
| Free trial | 30 days, up to $100 in usage credit on one server |
| Money-back guarantee | None advertised beyond the free trial |
| Best for | Developers, agencies and sysadmins who want granular server specs |

## What Kamatera actually is

Kamatera is an infrastructure-as-a-service cloud provider, not a traditional shared-hosting company. Instead of choosing between a handful of named plans, you build a server by picking each resource independently: CPU type and core count, RAM in GB increments, SSD storage in GB increments, and monthly traffic allowance. That configurability is the entire pitch — it's aimed at people who know roughly what specs their workload needs and don't want to overpay for a bundled plan that wastes half its resources.

This also means Kamatera isn't a beginner-friendly, one-click WordPress host out of the box. There's no bundled cPanel, Plesk, or custom dashboard pre-installed on the server — you get a clean OS image (a range of Linux distributions plus Windows Server options) and install whatever control panel or stack you want yourself, or run it headless via SSH.

## Pricing table

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check Kamatera's live pricing page before buying.

| Component | Starting cost |
|---|---|
| Base server (1 vCPU, 1GB RAM, 20GB SSD, 5TB traffic) | $4/month |
| Extra storage | ~$0.05/GB per month |
| Extra bandwidth | ~$0.01/GB |
| Hourly billing | Charged by the minute, only while the server runs |

Because every resource is priced independently, there isn't a single "plan" price beyond the entry tier — a server with more RAM, more vCPUs, or more storage costs proportionally more, and the total depends entirely on the configuration you assemble.

## Real cost breakdown

The advertised $4/month figure is a real, non-promotional starting price for the smallest possible configuration — there's no multi-year lock-in required to get it, unlike hosts that only offer their lowest headline price on a 24-48 month term. That said, $4/month buys very little (1 vCPU, 1GB RAM, 20GB storage), and most real workloads — a WordPress site with any meaningful traffic, a small app backend, a game server — will need more RAM or vCPUs, which raises the monthly cost above the headline figure quickly.

The 30-day free trial covers up to $100 of usage on one server, which is generous enough to actually build and load-test a realistic configuration rather than just kick the tires on the smallest tier. The trial does not require manually downgrading before it starts billing — but once the 30 days or the $100 credit runs out, whichever comes first, billing converts automatically at the standard rate for whatever configuration you left running. There's no published money-back guarantee beyond the trial itself, so treat the trial period as your actual evaluation window.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose the entry Availability tier (1 vCPU / 1GB RAM / 20GB SSD)** if you're running a lightweight dev/test box, a personal project, or a low-traffic static or brochure site.
- **Choose a mid-size custom configuration (2-4 vCPUs, 4-8GB RAM)** if you're hosting a production WordPress or small e-commerce site with real traffic, or running a small application backend.
- **Choose a larger, higher-CPU configuration** if you're running a database server, a build/CI box, or anything CPU-bound that needs dedicated compute rather than burstable resources.
- **Choose hourly billing** for short-lived workloads — testing, staging environments, or servers you spin up and tear down repeatedly — since you only pay while the server is powered on.
- **Choose monthly billing** for anything you intend to run continuously, since it's the simpler predictable-cost option.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| True per-component pricing — pay only for the CPU/RAM/storage/bandwidth you pick | No bundled control panel — requires comfort with server administration |
| Real $4/month entry price with no long-term contract required | Total cost is unpredictable until you finalize a configuration |
| Both hourly and monthly billing, with proration | No advertised money-back guarantee outside the trial |
| Generous 30-day / $100 free trial to test a real configuration | Trial converts to paid billing automatically when it ends |

## Support

Kamatera offers support through a ticketing system and, on higher usage tiers, more direct channels; it does not market a live-chat-first, beginner-oriented support experience the way budget shared hosts do. Customer feedback on independent review sites points to responsive, knowledgeable support for technical issues, which fits the platform's developer-oriented positioning — but don't expect hand-holding through basic server setup or control-panel configuration, since none is provided.

## Migration

Kamatera does not offer a "free migration" service comparable to hosts built around WordPress-specific site transfers. Moving an existing site to Kamatera means provisioning a new server, installing your own web server/database stack (or a control panel if you want one), and migrating files and databases manually or via your own tooling — a fundamentally different process than a shared-hosting migration wizard. Budget migration time and technical effort accordingly, especially if you're moving from a host that handled the server layer for you.

## Where it's a strong fit

Kamatera works well for developers and agencies who know their resource requirements and want to avoid overpaying for bundled specs they won't use. It's also a reasonable fit for short-lived or bursty workloads thanks to hourly billing, and for anyone who wants a real cloud VPS to experiment with during a genuinely useful free-trial window before committing.

## Where to think twice

If you want a beginner-friendly host with a control panel already installed, one-click app installs, and phone/live-chat support that walks you through setup, Kamatera is the wrong starting point — you'll be managing the server yourself from day one. It's also a weaker fit if you need a predictable flat monthly bill without doing any configuration math, since the final price depends entirely on the specs you choose.

## Bottom line

Kamatera delivers on its core promise: genuinely modular cloud VPS pricing with no bundled fat and no long-term contract requirement, backed by a free trial that's actually long and generous enough to test a real setup. It's a solid pick for developers and technically comfortable users who want control over server specs and cost — but it's not the place to start if you want a managed, control-panel-equipped host that handles the server layer for you.

## FAQs

**Does Kamatera include a control panel like cPanel?**
No. Kamatera provisions a bare server image, and installing cPanel, Plesk, or any other panel — or running headless — is up to you.

**What's the cheapest Kamatera server?**
The entry Availability-tier configuration starts at $4/month for 1 vCPU, 1GB RAM, 20GB NVMe SSD storage and 5TB of traffic.

**Does Kamatera have a free trial?**
Yes — new accounts get a 30-day free trial covering up to $100 of usage on one server, enough to build and test a realistic configuration.

**Is Kamatera billed monthly or hourly?**
Both. Monthly servers are prepaid with proration for mid-month changes, and hourly servers bill by the minute only while running, with no long-term contract either way.

**Does Kamatera offer a money-back guarantee?**
There's no separate money-back guarantee advertised beyond the free trial — treat the 30-day trial period as your evaluation window.

**Is Kamatera good for beginners?**
Not particularly. There's no bundled control panel or one-click app installer, so it suits developers and sysadmins more than someone who wants a managed, beginner-friendly dashboard.

**How does Kamatera pricing compare to fixed-plan hosts?**
Instead of choosing from a few named plans, you configure CPU, RAM, storage and bandwidth independently, so cost scales directly with the resources you pick rather than a bundled tier.

**Does Kamatera help migrate an existing site?**
No dedicated free-migration service is offered — moving a site means provisioning your own stack and migrating files/databases yourself or with your own tooling.
