author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Rocket.net good hosting?

Rocket.net is a solid pick if you run WordPress and want a global Cloudflare Enterprise CDN, a web application firewall and daily backups included on every plan without upselling. It's not a fit if you want cPanel, non-WordPress hosting, or the lowest possible entry price — Starter runs $30/month for one site.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $30/month (Starter, billed monthly) |
| Annual price | $300/year, with promotional annual offers available at signup |
| Renewal price | No price increase advertised at renewal |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days (Managed and Agency plans; excludes Enterprise) |
| Control panel | Proprietary Rocket.net panel (no cPanel) |
| Free migration | Yes, unlimited |
| Best for | WordPress sites that need CDN-level speed and security |

Pricing above was accurate as of September 18, 2026, and can change — check Rocket.net's current pricing page before buying.

## What Rocket.net actually is

Rocket.net is a managed WordPress-only host built directly on top of Cloudflare's Enterprise network rather than a generic data-center setup with a CDN bolted on afterward. Every plan — including the cheapest one — gets the Cloudflare Enterprise CDN, an enterprise-grade web application firewall, and edge caching baked in. There's no shared hosting for generic PHP sites, no email hosting bundle, and no cPanel; site management happens through a control panel Rocket.net built specifically for WordPress workflows.

That focus matters for who this is for. If you need to host a mix of static sites, a mail server, and a WordPress blog under one roof, Rocket.net isn't built for that. If you run WordPress and performance/security at the edge is the priority, it's built specifically around that use case.

## Pricing

| Plan | Sites | Storage | Visits | Monthly price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | 1 | 10GB | Unmetered | $30 |
| Pro | 3 | 20GB | Unmetered | $60 |
| Business | 10 | 40GB | Unmetered | $100 |
| Expert | 25 | 50GB | Unmetered | $200 |

Above Managed hosting, Rocket.net also sells Agency tiers (10-200+ sites, $100-$1,600+/month) for shops managing many client sites, and custom Enterprise plans starting around $649/month for larger operations with dedicated resource needs.

## The real cost breakdown

The list price on Starter is $30/month if you pay monthly, or $300/year on annual billing — Rocket.net's annual billing includes roughly two months free compared to paying monthly all year. Promotional signup pricing (commonly advertised as a heavily discounted first year) is available on top of that, so what you're quoted at checkout may be lower than list price for the first term.

The detail worth flagging either way: Rocket.net advertises no price increase at renewal, which is a real point of difference from budget hosts where the advertised price is only good for the first term and jumps significantly afterward. That said, Starter's $30/month list price is still well above entry-level shared hosting from budget providers — you're paying for the managed WordPress/Cloudflare stack, not competing on rock-bottom sticker price. Unlimited free migrations are included, so moving an existing site in doesn't carry a separate line-item cost.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Starter** if you're running a single WordPress site — a blog, small business site, or portfolio — and want CDN-backed performance and security without paying for multi-site capacity you won't use.
- **Choose Pro** if you manage two or three WordPress sites yourself and want more storage headroom than Starter's 10GB.
- **Choose Business** if you're running up to 10 sites, such as a small agency or a business with several brand microsites, and want the same enterprise CDN/WAF stack across all of them.
- **Choose Expert or an Agency tier** if you're managing 25+ WordPress sites for clients and need bulk-tier pricing and management tooling built for that scale.
- **Talk to sales about Enterprise** only if you have dedicated infrastructure or compliance requirements beyond what the standard tiers cover.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Cloudflare Enterprise CDN, WAF and edge caching on every plan, including Starter | WordPress-only — no general shared hosting or email hosting |
| No advertised price increase at renewal | Starter's $30/month is high next to budget shared hosting |
| Unlimited free migrations | No cPanel, so migrating configuration/habits from a cPanel host takes adjustment |
| Daily backups and staging environments included | Storage caps (10-50GB on Managed tiers) are modest versus unlimited-storage competitors |
| 24/7 support | 30-day guarantee excludes Enterprise plans |

## Support

Rocket.net advertises 24/7/365 support access. Because the platform is WordPress-specific, support is scoped to that stack rather than the broader mixed-hosting troubleshooting a generalist host's support team handles — in practice that tends to mean staff who are deeply familiar with WordPress performance and Cloudflare configuration issues specifically, rather than a wider but shallower support surface.

## Migration

Rocket.net includes unlimited free migrations for moving an existing WordPress site onto its platform, which removes a common friction point (and hidden cost) when switching hosts. As with any managed migration offer, it's worth confirming ahead of time what's included for more complex setups (multiple environments, custom server configs) versus a standard single-site move.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Running one or more WordPress sites where page-load speed and security at the edge are priorities.
- Wanting a CDN, WAF, and daily backups included by default rather than as paid add-ons.
- Willing to pay a premium managed-hosting price instead of shopping strictly on the lowest sticker price.
- Comfortable moving away from cPanel to a WordPress-specific control panel.

## Where to think twice

- You need to host non-WordPress sites, email, or general-purpose PHP applications.
- You're on a tight budget and Starter's $30/month is out of range for a single small site.
- You specifically want cPanel because your workflow or team is already built around it.
- You need storage well beyond 50GB on a mid-tier plan without moving to Agency/Enterprise pricing.

## Bottom line

Rocket.net earns its "managed WordPress + Cloudflare Enterprise" positioning — the CDN, WAF and daily backups genuinely ship on every tier rather than being reserved for the top of the price list, and the no-renewal-increase pricing model is a real advantage over hosts that quietly hike prices after the first term. It's not competing with budget shared hosting, and it shouldn't be judged against it — for a WordPress-only site where speed and edge security are the priority and the $30-and-up monthly price is acceptable, it's a strong option.

## FAQs

**Is Rocket.net only for WordPress?**
Yes — Rocket.net is a WordPress-specific managed host. It doesn't offer general shared hosting, email hosting, or hosting for other CMS platforms.

**Does Rocket.net use cPanel?**
No. Site management runs through Rocket.net's own control panel, built specifically around WordPress rather than the cPanel interface used by many other hosts.

**What's included in the Cloudflare Enterprise CDN?**
Every plan, including Starter, includes the Cloudflare Enterprise CDN, an enterprise-grade web application firewall, and edge caching served from Cloudflare's global network.

**How much does Rocket.net cost?**
Starter lists at $30/month billed monthly or $300/year billed annually, with promotional annual pricing sometimes available at signup. Higher tiers (Pro, Business, Expert) scale up in price alongside site count and storage.

**Will my price increase when I renew?**
Rocket.net advertises no price increase at renewal, unlike hosts whose lowest price only applies to an initial promotional term.

**Does Rocket.net offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — a 30-day money-back guarantee applies to Managed and Agency plans. Enterprise plans are excluded from this guarantee.

**Is migration to Rocket.net free?**
Yes, Rocket.net advertises unlimited free migrations for bringing an existing WordPress site onto its platform.

**Is Rocket.net good for a small single-site blog?**
It can be, if CDN-level speed and built-in security matter to you and the $30/month Starter price fits your budget — for a purely budget-focused single blog, cheaper shared hosting options exist, just without the same Cloudflare Enterprise stack.

title: Vultr Review 2026: VPS Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: Vultr's cloud VPS pricing, hourly billing, data centers and lack of a bundled control panel — is it right for developers vs. beginners?
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is Vultr a good choice for hosting?

Vultr is a solid choice if you want raw cloud compute you configure yourself — not a beginner web host. It offers hourly-billed VPS instances from $2.50/month, 33 global data center regions, and no bundled control panel, making it best suited to developers, agencies, and anyone comfortable managing a server over SSH.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $2.50/month (512MB RAM, IPv6-only) |
| Common entry tier | $6/month (1GB RAM, High Frequency, NVMe) |
| Billing model | Hourly, capped at the monthly rate |
| Control panel | None bundled (self-managed, or add cPanel/Plesk yourself) |
| Data center regions | ~33 locations across ~20 countries |
| Money-back guarantee | None blanket — billing is on-demand/usage-based |
| Best for | Developers, agencies, self-managed infrastructure |

## What Vultr actually is

Vultr is a cloud infrastructure provider, not a shared web host. When you sign up, you're provisioning a virtual private server (or bare metal, or GPU instance) with root access to a blank Linux or Windows box — there's no hPanel, no cPanel, no pre-installed WordPress dashboard waiting for you. You choose the OS image, the region, and the resources, and everything after that — web server setup, database installation, TLS certificates, backups, security patching — is on you, or on whatever software stack you choose to install.

That's a meaningfully different product from something like Hostinger or Namecheap's shared hosting, which sell a managed environment aimed at getting a WordPress site live in minutes with a support team behind it. Vultr sells the underlying compute layer developers use to build that themselves, or to run applications, APIs, game servers, or anything else needing a dedicated instance with predictable, hourly-metered pricing.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this review's publish date and can change — check Vultr's current pricing page before purchasing, since cloud providers frequently adjust rates and add new instance types.

| Plan | vCPU | RAM | Storage | Bandwidth | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regular Performance (IPv6) | 1 | 512MB | 10GB SSD | 0.5TB | $2.50/month |
| Regular Performance (IPv4) | 1 | 512MB | 10GB SSD | 0.5TB | $3.50/month |
| High Frequency | 1 | 1GB | 25GB NVMe | 2TB | $6.00/month |
| High Frequency | 1 | 2GB | 50GB NVMe | 3TB | $12.00/month |

These are Vultr's Cloud Compute lines; larger instances (more vCPU/RAM), Optimized Cloud Compute, Bare Metal, and Cloud GPU plans scale well beyond this table for production workloads.

## The real cost breakdown

Vultr's pricing model is genuinely different from a typical annual-contract host, and it cuts both ways.

- **Hourly billing, monthly cap.** You're charged per hour of actual usage, but that hourly rate stops accumulating once it reaches the plan's listed monthly price — so an instance left running all month costs exactly the advertised monthly figure, and one you spin up for a few days costs only those days.
- **No long-term lock-in discount trap.** There's no "$2.99/month if you prepay 48 months, then it jumps to $11" dynamic here. You pay for what you provision, when you provision it. That also means there's no deep multi-year discount to chase — the sticker price is close to the real price.
- **Bandwidth overage is the real gotcha.** Each plan includes a fixed bandwidth allowance. Go over it and Vultr bills overage at $0.01 per GB in most North American and Western European regions, rising to $0.025/GB in Singapore/Tokyo and $0.05/GB in Sydney. A low-traffic project is unlikely to hit this, but a growing app or traffic spike can turn a $6/month instance into a larger bill if bandwidth isn't monitored.
- **No control panel license included.** If you want cPanel or Plesk on top of a Vultr instance, that's a separate paid license — factor it in if you're not comfortable managing a server purely from the command line.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose the $2.50-3.50/month Regular Performance tier** if you're testing something small — a personal script, a low-traffic side project, or learning Linux server administration — where raw performance doesn't matter yet.
- **Choose a $6-12/month High Frequency plan** if you're running a real (if modest) production workload — a small API, a lightweight app backend, or a self-managed WordPress site where you're comfortable configuring your own web server and database.
- **Look at Optimized Cloud Compute or higher-RAM tiers** if you're running anything with sustained CPU/memory demand — multiple services, a growing user base, or workloads where the entry NVMe tiers would bottleneck.
- **Consider Bare Metal or Cloud GPU** only if you have a specific need for dedicated hardware or GPU-accelerated workloads (ML training/inference, rendering) — these are priced and positioned well beyond a typical website hosting budget.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Hourly billing with a hard monthly cap — no overpaying for partial usage | No bundled control panel — real server admin skill required |
| Entry pricing from $2.50/month | Bandwidth overage charges can add up if traffic spikes go unmonitored |
| ~33 data center regions across ~20 countries | Not beginner-friendly — no guided setup for non-technical users |
| No forced long-term contract to get a reasonable rate | No blanket money-back guarantee since billing is usage-based |

## Support

Vultr's support is oriented around infrastructure, not hand-holding a website build. Expect ticket-based support and a documentation-driven help center rather than the 24/7 live-chat-walks-you-through-WordPress model shared hosts market. If you need someone to fix a plugin conflict or email setup, that's outside what a raw VPS provider's support desk typically handles — you (or a developer you hire) own the application layer.

## Migration

Moving an existing site or app onto Vultr means self-managed migration: provisioning a new instance, installing your stack, moving files and databases over yourself, pointing DNS at the new IP, and validating everything before decommissioning the old host. There's no "we'll migrate your site for you" concierge service built into the base product. Anyone without server administration experience should budget for a developer's time before committing.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Developers and agencies who want full root control over their server environment
- Projects needing specific data center geography — 33 regions gives good options for latency-sensitive apps serving a global or regional audience
- Workloads with variable, bursty usage that benefit from hourly billing instead of a flat annual contract
- Anyone already comfortable with Linux administration who wants to avoid shared-hosting resource limits

## Where to think twice

- Non-technical users who want a website live without touching a terminal — this is the wrong product category entirely
- Anyone expecting an included control panel, one-click app installs, or hands-on support for application-level issues
- High-bandwidth, high-traffic sites without a plan to monitor usage against the overage thresholds
- Businesses that specifically want a fixed, predictable bill regardless of usage patterns

## Bottom line

Vultr does what it says: cheap, flexible, hourly-billed cloud compute with a wide spread of global regions, aimed at people who want to run their own server stack rather than rent a managed website. It is not a replacement for cPanel-based shared hosting, and treating it like one — expecting guided setup or application-level support — will lead to a frustrating experience. For developers who know what they're deploying, the pricing model and data center spread make it worth evaluating alongside other self-managed VPS providers.

## FAQs

**Does Vultr include a free domain?**
No. Vultr sells compute infrastructure, not domain registration or bundled extras like a free domain — you'll need to register a domain separately and point its DNS at your instance.

**Can I install cPanel on a Vultr VPS?**
Yes, but it's not included — cPanel and similar panels (like Plesk) require their own separate paid license that you purchase and install on top of the base instance.

**Is Vultr good for beginners?**
Not particularly. Vultr assumes you're comfortable with SSH, Linux server administration, and managing your own software stack. Beginners wanting a guided, supported website setup are generally better served by a managed shared host.

**How does Vultr's hourly billing actually work?**
You're charged per hour of usage, but the hourly rate is capped once it reaches your plan's listed monthly price — so running an instance continuously for a full month never costs more than the advertised monthly figure, while short-lived instances cost only for the hours used.

**What happens if I exceed my bandwidth allowance?**
Vultr charges an overage fee per GB beyond your plan's included bandwidth — $0.01/GB in most North American and Western European regions, with higher per-GB rates in select Asia-Pacific regions like Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney.

**Does Vultr offer a money-back guarantee?**
Vultr doesn't advertise a blanket refund window the way fixed-term shared hosts do; billing is usage-based, so review current account and billing terms before adding a large credit balance.

**How many data centers does Vultr have?**
Around 33 data center regions spread across roughly 20 countries as of its most recent regional expansion in 2026, one of the broader independent-cloud footprints available.

**Is Vultr cheaper than a managed shared host?**
It can be for technical users who don't need bundled features like a control panel or one-click app installs, since you're paying purely for compute. But once you factor in your own time (or a developer's time) to manage the server, it isn't necessarily "cheaper" for a non-technical site owner.

Looking for a discount on your next plan? Check the [Vultr coupon page](/coupons/vultr) for current offers, or browse more [web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

|---|---|
| Starting price | Free (Personal from $4/mo annual, $9/mo monthly) |
| Renewal price | Personal $9/mo, Premium $18/mo, Business $40/mo, Commerce $70/mo (monthly billing) |
| Money-back guarantee | 14 days (annual/2-yr/3-yr plans), 7 days (monthly plans) |
| Best for | Bloggers, small business sites, writers who don't want to manage a server |
| Trustpilot rating | 3.7/5 from 4,156 reviews |

## What WordPress.com actually is

WordPress.com is a hosted platform built and run by Automattic (the company behind much of the core WordPress open-source project). It's easy to confuse with WordPress.org, and the difference matters:

- **WordPress.org** is free, open-source software. You download it and install it on hosting you choose — a shared plan, a VPS, or a managed WordPress host like Kinsta or WP Engine. You get full control over plugins, themes, server configuration and code.
- **WordPress.com** is a managed service. Automattic runs the servers, handles updates and security, and gives you a dashboard to build a site. In exchange, you give up some flexibility: on lower tiers you're choosing from a curated plugin/theme ecosystem rather than uploading any file you want.

If someone tells you "I built my site on WordPress" without specifying which one, that ambiguity is exactly why this distinction gets confusing — and it's worth checking before you commit to either path.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of this post's publish date and can change — check WordPress.com's own pricing page for the current live rate before buying.

| Plan | Monthly billing | Annual (per mo) | Storage | Key inclusion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | $0 | 1GB | Subdomain only, no plugins, no custom domain |
| Personal | $9 | $4 | 6GB | Free domain (1 yr), plugins, ad-free |
| Premium | $18 | $8 | 13GB | Premium themes, video hosting, payment buttons |
| Business | $40 | $25 | 50GB | Priority 24/7 support, staging sites, SFTP/DB access |
| Commerce | $70 | $45 | 50GB | Full WooCommerce, 0% transaction fees, sell in 60+ countries |

## The real cost breakdown

The headline "per month" price you see on the pricing page assumes you pay for a full year (or longer) upfront. Pay monthly instead and the same Personal plan jumps from $4/month to $9/month — more than double. There's no confusing multi-year renewal cliff like you'll find on some budget shared hosts, but the annual-vs-monthly gap is still real: committing to a year upfront more than halves the effective monthly cost on every paid tier.

Add-on costs to budget for: a custom domain (free for the first year on Personal and up, then renews at standard domain pricing), and any premium theme or plugin you buy separately from WordPress.com's own marketplace — the base plan price doesn't include third-party premium add-ons.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Free** if you're testing WordPress.com out or building a hobby blog on a wordpress.com subdomain and don't need a custom domain or plugins yet.
- **Choose Personal** if you want a real custom domain and a simple blog, portfolio or small brochure site with basic plugin access — this is the entry point where WordPress.com starts feeling like a "real" website.
- **Choose Premium** if you want premium theme designs, want to host video directly, or need simple PayPal/Stripe payment buttons without a full store.
- **Choose Business** if you're running a client site, a small business site that needs staging environments before pushing changes live, or you want direct SFTP/database access alongside priority support.
- **Choose Commerce** if you're actually selling products and want WooCommerce built in with 0% WordPress.com transaction fees, rather than bolting ecommerce onto a lower tier.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Free tier to start with no card required | Free plan has no custom domain, no plugins, and shows WordPress.com branding |
| Zero server maintenance — updates and security handled for you | Lower tiers are limited to WordPress.com's curated plugin ecosystem, not arbitrary uploads |
| Annual pricing is meaningfully cheaper than monthly | Monthly pricing is steep by comparison ($9-$70/mo) |
| Business plan adds staging sites and direct SFTP/database access | Migrating a site out later means exporting content, not just moving files |
| Commerce plan bundles WooCommerce with 0% WordPress.com fees | Full ecommerce requires the most expensive tier |

## Support

Support channels scale with plan tier. Business and Commerce subscribers get priority 24/7 live chat support. Lower paid tiers (Personal, Premium) still get access to support but without the same priority queue. There's no phone support tier advertised — support is chat- and documentation-based across the board, backed by WordPress.com's own extensive help library.

## Migration

Migrating onto or off WordPress.com is genuinely different from typical hosting migration, and it's worth understanding before you commit either direction:

- **Migrating in** from a self-hosted WordPress.org site: WordPress.com offers import tools that bring over content, but a site with many custom plugins or a heavily customized theme may not translate cleanly, since those plugins likely aren't available in WordPress.com's ecosystem.
- **Migrating out** to self-hosted WordPress.org: you can export your content (posts, pages, media) through WordPress's built-in export tool, but you're rebuilding the plugin/theme setup from scratch on the new host rather than just copying files over, because WordPress.com's own infrastructure and any WordPress.com-specific features don't carry over.

If you expect to switch platforms later, factor in that this isn't a simple "move the files" job the way switching between two self-hosted WordPress.org hosts usually is.

## Where it's a strong fit

WordPress.com is a strong fit for bloggers, writers, portfolio sites, and small businesses that want a real website without managing a server, applying security updates, or troubleshooting hosting issues themselves. The free-to-paid ladder also makes it easy to start at zero cost and upgrade only once you actually need a custom domain or more capability.

## Where to think twice

Think twice if you need a specific third-party plugin outside WordPress.com's ecosystem, want full server-level control, or are already comfortable managing a self-hosted WordPress.org install — in those cases a regular host (shared, VPS, or managed WordPress hosting) will give you more flexibility for often less money at the mid tier.

## Bottom line

WordPress.com earns its place as a managed, low-maintenance way to run a WordPress-powered site, especially for anyone who doesn't want to think about server administration. The free tier and reasonably priced Personal/Premium plans make it easy to start small, but the plugin ecosystem restriction on lower tiers and the annual-vs-monthly pricing gap are worth understanding going in — they're the two things most likely to surprise someone expecting it to behave exactly like self-hosted WordPress.org.

## FAQs

**Is WordPress.com free?**
Yes, there's a free plan with 1GB storage on a wordpress.com subdomain, but it has no custom domain, no plugins, and displays WordPress.com branding. Most people building a real site upgrade to at least Personal.

**What's the difference between WordPress.com and WordPress.org?**
WordPress.org is free open-source software you install on hosting of your choice with full control. WordPress.com is a managed platform run by Automattic that hosts and runs WordPress for you, trading some flexibility for zero server maintenance.

**Can I install any plugin I want on WordPress.com?**
Plugin installation is available starting on the Personal plan, but you're choosing from WordPress.com's own plugin directory rather than uploading arbitrary third-party plugin files, unlike self-hosted WordPress.org.

**Does WordPress.com offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes — 14 days on annual, two-year and three-year plans, and 7 days on monthly plans, with refunds not prorated.

**Can I sell products on WordPress.com?**
Yes, most fully on the Commerce plan, which bundles WooCommerce with 0% WordPress.com transaction fees and support for selling in 60+ countries. The Premium plan only supports basic PayPal/Stripe payment buttons.

**Is WordPress.com good for beginners?**
Yes — the managed nature of the platform (no server setup, automatic updates, built-in themes) makes it one of the more beginner-friendly ways to get a WordPress site online without prior hosting experience.

**How much does WordPress.com cost per month?**
Paying annually, Personal starts at $4/month, Premium at $8/month, Business at $25/month and Commerce at $45/month. Paying monthly instead, those same plans cost $9, $18, $40 and $70 respectively.

**Is migrating away from WordPress.com difficult?**
It's more involved than typical hosting migration. You can export your content through WordPress's built-in export tool, but plugins, themes and WordPress.com-specific features don't carry over — you rebuild that part on the new host.

Ready to compare pricing? Check the [WordPress.com coupon page](/coupons/wordpresscom) or browse more [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting).

title: WP Engine Review 2026: Pricing, Features and Verdict
excerpt: WP Engine review: managed WordPress hosting pricing, visit limits, overage fees, migration, support and whether it's worth the premium price.
author: Editorial Team
body:
## Is WP Engine worth it?

WP Engine is a good fit if you want managed WordPress hosting with strong caching, staging environments and a WordPress-only support team, and you're comfortable paying more than a shared host in exchange for not managing server-level maintenance yourself. It's a weaker fit if your traffic is unpredictable, since plans are priced around a monthly visit allowance rather than unlimited bandwidth.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $28/month (Essential, billed annually) |
| Entry-tier limits | 1-30 sites, 25,000-400,000 visits/mo, 10-50GB storage |
| Overage cost | $2 per 1,000 extra monthly visitors |
| Control panel | Proprietary "User Portal" (not cPanel) |
| Money-back guarantee | 60 days (annual plans) |
| Free migration | Yes, via automated plugin on Essential |
| Best for | WordPress sites that want managed hosting without server admin work |

Pricing above reflects WP Engine's publicly listed plans as of September 2026 and can change — check [WP Engine's coupon page](/coupons/wpengine) for current offers before buying.

## What WP Engine actually is

WP Engine is a managed WordPress hosting platform — it only hosts WordPress, not general-purpose sites, email or other CMSs. Instead of handing you cPanel and a generic LAMP stack, it runs its own infrastructure tuned specifically for WordPress: built-in caching layers, a CDN, automated daily backups, one-click staging environments, and a proprietary web dashboard called the User Portal for managing all of it. The pitch is that WP Engine handles the server administration — security patching, performance tuning, uptime monitoring — so the site owner focuses on content and design rather than infrastructure.

This positions WP Engine well above budget shared hosts like Hostinger or Namecheap's Stellar tiers, both in price and in what's actually managed for you. It's closer to a premium tier aimed at agencies, businesses and serious WordPress publishers than at someone launching a first blog on a shoestring budget.

## Pricing

| Plan | Sites | Monthly visits | Storage | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Essential | 1-30 | 25,000-400,000 | 10-50GB | From $28/month (annual billing) |
| Core | 30-50 | 400,000-800,000 | 50GB-2TB | Custom quote (contact sales) |
| Enterprise | 50+ | 800,000+ | 2TB+ | Custom quote (contact sales) |

Essential is the only self-service tier with published pricing; Core and Enterprise use isolated resources and require talking to WP Engine's sales team for a quote, which is typical of hosts targeting higher-traffic or agency accounts rather than solo site owners.

## The real cost breakdown

The $28/month figure for Essential is the annual-billing rate, and WP Engine layers a further 20% first-year discount for new customers on top of that at various points — meaning the number you see on the plans page may already be a promotional rate rather than the flat go-forward price. Because WP Engine doesn't publish month-to-month Essential pricing as prominently as the annual rate, and because the discount structure shifts, it's worth confirming the exact checkout total (including tax) before committing to a term.

The bigger cost variable isn't the base plan — it's overage. Every Essential-and-up tier caps monthly visits, and going over that cap doesn't get your site suspended; instead WP Engine bills $2 per 1,000 extra visitors. A site that spikes from a viral post or a seasonal traffic surge can see a real bill increase in that month even while staying on the same nominal plan. If your traffic is lumpy or growing fast, budget for overage rather than assuming the sticker price is the ceiling.

## Which plan should you choose

Choose Essential if you're running one to a handful of WordPress sites with moderate, fairly predictable traffic — freelancer portfolios, small business sites, or a blog that isn't yet pulling hundreds of thousands of monthly visits. It covers the core managed-WordPress feature set (staging, backups, CDN, free migration plugin) without needing a sales call.

Choose Core if you're running an agency with 30+ client sites, need isolated resources instead of shared infrastructure, or your traffic has already outgrown Essential's 400,000-visit ceiling. You'll need to contact sales for pricing, but the isolated-resource model reduces noisy-neighbor risk that shared-tier hosting can't fully avoid.

Choose Enterprise only if you're operating at real scale — 50+ sites or 800,000+ monthly visits — where dedicated infrastructure and a named account team matter more than self-service simplicity.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| WordPress-specialized support team | No cPanel — proprietary User Portal has a learning curve |
| Free automated migration plugin | Visit-based pricing means overage risk on traffic spikes |
| Staging environments and daily backups included | Core/Enterprise pricing isn't public — requires a sales call |
| 60-day money-back guarantee on annual plans | Meaningfully pricier than budget shared hosts |
| Isolated resources at Core and above | WordPress-only — no flexibility for other platforms |

## Support

WP Engine's support is staffed by WordPress specialists rather than generalist hosting agents, which matters if an issue is plugin- or theme-specific rather than purely a server problem. Support channels are accessed through the User Portal rather than a traditional helpdesk ticket system tied to a cPanel account.

## Migration

Essential-tier customers get a free automated migration plugin that pulls a WordPress site in from almost any other host, handling files, database and settings transfer without manual server work. Core and Enterprise customers instead get managed, white-glove migration handled by WP Engine's team, which fits the higher-touch, higher-cost profile of those tiers.

## Where it's a strong fit

WP Engine works well for WordPress-only site owners who want to stop thinking about server maintenance, agencies managing multiple client sites who need staging and backup workflows built in, and businesses whose traffic is high enough to justify managed infrastructure but who don't want to run their own DevOps team.

## Where to think twice

If your budget is tight, or you run more than one CMS, or your traffic pattern is unpredictable enough that overage fees would be a recurring surprise, WP Engine's model works against you. A budget shared host with unmetered bandwidth, or a VPS you manage yourself, may be more appropriate if per-visit cost predictability matters more than managed convenience.

## Bottom line

WP Engine delivers what it promises for a specific audience: hands-off, WordPress-specialized managed hosting with real infrastructure behind it, at a price point that reflects that specialization rather than a budget shared-hosting rate. The visit-based pricing model is the main thing to plan around — it rewards predictable traffic and can surprise you if it isn't. For agencies and WordPress-committed businesses that value staging, backups and specialized support over the lowest possible sticker price, it's a reasonable premium option; for a first small blog on a tight budget, a cheaper generalist host is the more sensible starting point.

## FAQs

**Is WP Engine good for beginners?**
It's usable for beginners, but the value proposition assumes you're specifically committed to WordPress and want managed infrastructure rather than the cheapest possible entry price — a $3-5/month shared host is a gentler starting point if budget is the main constraint.

**Does WP Engine use cPanel?**
No — WP Engine built its own proprietary User Portal for site and account management instead of offering cPanel.

**What happens if my site exceeds its visit limit?**
WP Engine charges an overage fee of $2 per 1,000 extra monthly visitors rather than suspending the site, so a traffic spike results in a higher bill rather than downtime.

**Can I host non-WordPress sites on WP Engine?**
No — WP Engine is a WordPress-only managed hosting platform; it isn't built for other CMSs or general-purpose hosting.

**Is there a free trial?**
WP Engine doesn't advertise a free trial on Essential, but it does offer a 60-day money-back guarantee on annual billing, which functions as a longer-than-typical risk window to test the service.

**Does WP Engine offer free migration?**
Yes, on the Essential tier via a free automated migration plugin; Core and Enterprise customers get managed migration handled directly by WP Engine's team.

**How does WP Engine compare to budget shared hosts?**
WP Engine is priced and positioned well above budget shared hosts — it's a managed, WordPress-specialized platform with staging, backups and specialist support built in, not a bare-bones cPanel shared plan. See [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to compare it against budget alternatives.

**Is WP Engine's Essential price the final renewal rate?**
Not necessarily — WP Engine layers first-year new-customer discounts on top of the listed annual-billing rate at times, so the exact ongoing rate is worth confirming at checkout rather than assuming the listed price holds indefinitely.

body:
## Is WPX Hosting worth it in 2026?

WPX is a managed WordPress host built around fast support and a proprietary control panel rather than cPanel. It's a solid pick if you want quick live-chat responses and don't mind paying more than budget shared hosts, but its entry price is high for a single small site and there's no long-term prepaid discount cliff to chase.

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $17.99/mo (monthly billing), $14.99/mo (paid annually) |
| Renewal price | Generally matches the billing-term rate you chose — no sharp renewal hike |
| Control panel | Proprietary WPX Control Panel (not cPanel) |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Free migration | Yes |
| Best for | Sites that value fast support and speed over rock-bottom pricing |

## What WPX actually is

WPX is a managed WordPress hosting provider — it doesn't sell generic shared cPanel hosting, and every plan is built specifically to run WordPress sites. Instead of licensing cPanel (which WPX says adds server overhead), it built its own proprietary WPX Control Panel to handle domains, backups, staging environments, email and CDN settings in one interface. The company leans heavily on support speed as its main differentiator, publishing specific response-time claims rather than vague "24/7 support" language.

Every plan includes a free custom CDN (branded XDN) with 43 global endpoints, unlimited visitors regardless of tier, free SSL, and free migration of an existing WordPress site.

## Pricing

Pricing was accurate as of September 2026 and can change — check WPX's own pricing page before buying.

| Plan | Monthly billing | Annual billing (per mo) | Storage | Bandwidth | Websites |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $17.99 | $14.99 | 10 GB | 100 GB | 1 |
| Business | $29.99 | $24.99 | 20 GB | 200 GB | Up to 5 |
| Professional | $59.99 | $49.99 | 40 GB | 400 GB | Up to 15 |
| Elite | $119.99 | $99.99 | 80 GB | Unlimited | Up to 35 |
| Agency | $599.99 | $499.99 | 300 GB | Unlimited | Up to 200 |

## The real cost breakdown

WPX doesn't run the same "cheap intro price, painful renewal" model that a lot of shared hosts do. There's no headline $2-3/month teaser rate — Starter's cheapest published rate is $14.99/month, and that requires paying for a full year upfront. Paying monthly instead costs $17.99/month with no annual commitment.

Where WPX differs from budget hosts is what happens after the first term: the renewal rate generally lines up with whichever billing term you originally picked, rather than jumping to a much higher default price the way some shared-hosting renewals do. That makes WPX's total cost more predictable, but it also means there's no artificially low bait price to chase in the first place — you're paying a premium-tier rate from day one.

Bandwidth and storage limits step up meaningfully between tiers, so upgrading isn't just about wanting more websites — a single high-traffic site can outgrow Starter's 100GB bandwidth allowance and need Business or Professional even with just one domain.

## Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Starter** if you're running exactly one WordPress site with modest traffic and 10GB of storage is enough for your media library.
- **Choose Business** if you manage a handful of client or personal sites (up to 5) and want more breathing room on bandwidth and storage.
- **Choose Professional** if you're an agency or freelancer managing up to 15 sites, or a single site outgrowing Business's 200GB bandwidth cap.
- **Choose Elite** if you need unlimited bandwidth and are hosting up to 35 sites — this is where the bandwidth ceiling disappears.
- **Choose Agency** only if you're managing a large portfolio (up to 200 sites) and the per-site cost still pencils out against running smaller accounts separately.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Support-speed claims are specific (30-second average live-chat response, 15-minute average case resolution) | Entry price is high compared to budget shared hosts for a single small site |
| Renewal pricing generally matches the original billing term instead of spiking | No true budget tier — cheapest plan starts near $15-18/month |
| Free migration included on every plan | Storage and bandwidth caps are tighter at the low end (Starter: 10GB / 100GB) than some unlimited-storage competitors |
| Proprietary control panel is fast and simple | Not cPanel — workflows or tools built around cPanel don't transfer directly |
| Free CDN (XDN) with 43 endpoints on every plan | WordPress-only — not a general-purpose hosting platform for other CMS or app stacks |

## Support

WPX's headline differentiator is support speed, not just availability. The company publishes concrete claims — a 30-second average live-chat response time and a 15-minute average case resolution time — rather than the generic "24/7 support" most hosts advertise. Live chat is the primary channel, backed by a ticketing system for more involved issues. Whether every single interaction hits those averages will vary, but WPX treats support responsiveness as a core product feature rather than an afterthought, and it shows up consistently in customer feedback.

## Migration

WPX includes free migration of an existing WordPress site when you sign up, handled by its own team rather than a self-service plugin-only process. This is included at every plan tier, not gated behind the higher tiers, which matters if you're moving an established site with a real audience and don't want to risk downtime doing it yourself.

## Where it's a strong fit

- Freelancers and agencies managing multiple WordPress client sites who want fast support turnaround when something breaks on a client's site.
- Site owners who've been burned by slow support elsewhere and are willing to pay a premium for responsiveness.
- Anyone who wants out of cPanel's complexity without giving up core management features.

## Where to think twice

- Anyone hosting a single low-traffic site on a tight budget — WPX's entry price is well above bargain shared hosts.
- Sites running anything other than WordPress — WPX is WordPress-specific, not general-purpose hosting.
- Users who specifically need cPanel for compatibility with existing tools, scripts, or workflows.

## Bottom line

WPX earns its reputation on support speed and a clean, fast proprietary control panel rather than on being the cheapest option on the market. Its pricing model is also more honest than many budget hosts — renewal rates broadly track what you originally signed up for instead of quietly tripling. If responsive support and predictable renewal pricing matter more to you than the lowest possible entry price, WPX is a reasonable pick for WordPress-only hosting. If you're price-sensitive and running a single small site, its $14.99-$17.99/month starting point is hard to justify next to budget shared hosts charging a fraction of that.

## FAQs

**Does WPX Hosting use cPanel?**
No. WPX built its own proprietary WPX Control Panel instead of licensing cPanel, covering domains, backups, staging, email and CDN settings in a simplified interface.

**How much does WPX cost?**
Starter begins at $17.99/month billed monthly, or $14.99/month if paid annually. Higher tiers (Business, Professional, Elite, Agency) scale up from there based on site count, storage and bandwidth needs.

**Does WPX's price increase sharply at renewal?**
Generally not by much — WPX's renewal rate tends to match the billing term you originally chose, unlike hosts that advertise a low first-term price and renew several times higher.

**Is WPX good for beginners?**
WPX's control panel is simpler than cPanel, but the pricing and WordPress-only focus make it better suited to users who already have a site to move or specific support-speed needs, rather than someone building their very first website on the tightest possible budget.

**Does WPX offer a money-back guarantee?**
Yes, WPX backs its hosting plans with a 30-day money-back guarantee.

**Does WPX include free migration?**
Yes, free migration of an existing WordPress site is included on every plan tier.

**What is WPX's support response time?**
WPX advertises a 30-second average live-chat response time and a 15-minute average case resolution time as its core support differentiator.

**Can I host non-WordPress sites on WPX?**
No — WPX is a WordPress-specific managed hosting provider, not general-purpose hosting for other platforms.
